subject: biology
title: Sliding Filament Adventure
welcome_lead: Today you'll slide actin past myosin using the sliding filament theory.
meta_desc: A-Level Biology Muscle Contraction — sliding filament theory, Ca2+, troponin, tropomyosin, cross-bridges and ATP hydrolysis.
final_note: You learned that Ca2+ binds troponin, moves tropomyosin off actin's myosin-binding sites, and how the cross-bridge cycle uses ATP to slide actin past myosin and shorten the sarcomere.

concepts.def: Sarcomeres shorten as thin filaments slide past thick filaments
Protein blocking myosin-binding sites on actin at rest
Calcium-binding protein that moves tropomyosin when Ca2+ binds
Connection formed when a myosin head binds an actin site
Myosin head pivots, dragging actin towards centre of sarcomere
Releases energy for the power stroke and detaches the myosin head

walkthroughs.body_html:
At rest, tropomyosin covers myosin-binding sites on actin — no contraction can happen.

An action potential at the neuromuscular junction triggers release of Ca²⁺ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

Ca²⁺ binds troponin. Troponin changes shape and pulls tropomyosin off the binding sites.

Now myosin can attach.

Each myosin head goes through a cycle:

1. Head binds actin → cross-bridge forms.
2. ADP and Pi released → head pivots (power stroke) → drags actin towards centre.
3. New ATP binds myosin → head detaches.
4. ATP hydrolysed to ADP + Pi → head 'cocks back' ready to attach again.

Many heads cycle out of phase — like rowers pulling a boat.

Muscle needs ATP fast. Sources:
- Direct ATP (used in ~3 seconds)
- Phosphocreatine + ADP → ATP + creatine (~10 seconds)
- Anaerobic respiration → lactate (~1 minute)
- Aerobic respiration → long-term

Without ATP, myosin heads cannot detach → rigor mortis after death.

When Ca²⁺ is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum (active transport), tropomyosin returns to its blocking position → relaxation.

Contraction needs Ca²⁺ AND ATP.
